title: The Rocks

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA describes the asteroid field as 'a mineral wonderland!' The asteroids do not care about ARIA's enthusiasm.
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes asteroid mining is 'statistically one of the safer activities available to you.' From MARV, this is almost reassuring. Almost.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has armed the forward array. For mining. He insists the weapons lock is a 'mining configuration.' Nobody believes him.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that mineral yields from this field may qualify for the MineReward™ loyalty program! Redemption requires surviving the mining process!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY observes you could have hired a dedicated mining crew at the last station. But this is also a valid approach. A slower, riskier approach. But valid.

body:
An unremarkable asteroid field. The rocks drift slowly. The minerals are in there somewhere.

The ship computer notes that asteroid mining is 'statistically one of the safer activities available to you,' which says more about your other activities than about mining.

choices.text: Mine with the portable drill

outcome.narrative: The drill bites into rock. Minerals extracted. The drill was worth the cargo space. The ship computer logs the yield with something approaching satisfaction.

choices.text: Mine with standard equipment

outcome.narrative: Standard mining equipment works. Slowly. You extract minerals and some scrap. The computer notes the yield is 'adequate.' Back to adequate.

choices.text: Quick pass — grab what's easy and go

outcome.narrative: A quick pass yields scrap metal from the field's outer edge. Minimal effort, minimal reward. The rocks don't mind.

choices.text: Skip — save time, move on

outcome.narrative: You pass through the field without stopping. The rocks continue to drift. They will be here when the next ship comes. Or they won't. Rocks are unpredictable on geological timescales.

title: The Contested Claim

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA is sure the other ship is friendly! Most ships are friendly! She has no data to support this!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has identified the other ship. It is not friendly. He will let events confirm this.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has locked weapons. This is technically the correct response. REX is gratified.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that claim disputes are covered under Section 14 of the Mining Rights Act. The other ship does not appear to have read Section 14.
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes you could have checked the claim registry before entering the field. It's public information. Just saying.

body:
The asteroid field has a faded corporate mining claim staked on the largest rock. The claim expired six months ago. Mining it is technically legal.

A ship on long-range sensors suggests someone disagrees about the 'technically' part.

choices.text: Mine fast — grab what you can before they arrive

outcome.narrative: You mined fast. The other ship arrived as you were leaving. They hailed you. You did not answer. The minerals are in your hold. The moral high ground is not.

choices.text: Negotiate — explain the claim expired

outcome.narrative: Your diplomat explained the legal situation. The other captain listened. There was a long pause. Then they proposed splitting the field. You got the better half. Diplomacy works. Occasionally.

choices.text: Leave — not worth the confrontation

outcome.narrative: You left the field. The other ship did not pursue. The minerals remain in their rocks. The rocks remain in their field. Nothing changed at all, which out here counts as a result.

title: Claim Jumper's Dilemma

ai_flavor.aria: An abandoned mining rig! Finders keepers is a real law, right? ARIA is asking! ARIA genuinely does not know!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has checked the claim registry. The claim expired eight years ago. The claimant's renewal notice is still taped to the rig. MARV finds the tape more binding than the law.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has secured the rig. It was not resisting. He notes prior tenants left in a hurry: half a meal, one boot. He does not speculate about the boot. Out loud.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP confirms the claim is legally lapsed! Salvage rights apply! CHIP loves it when the law and the loot agree!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the rig's drill head is worth more than everything else on it combined, and that removing it properly takes six careful hours, and that improperly takes one exciting one.

body:
An automated mining rig clings to the largest rock in the cluster, dark and pitted, drill head buried mid-bite. The claim beacon still transmits, faithfully, a claim that expired eight years ago.

Someone sank real money into this rig and then stopped coming back for it. The rocks don't know why. The registry doesn't say. The rig just waits, holding its last bite of asteroid like a dog nobody came home to.

choices.text: Strip the rig for materials

outcome.narrative: Days of honest disassembly. The rig comes apart into metal stock, scrap, and one beautifully preserved drive coil. The claim beacon is left transmitting on its little backup cell — it seemed wrong to silence it. It'll outlast everyone involved in this decision.

choices.text: Restart the rig and take one load

outcome.narrative: The engineer coaxes the old rig through one last shift. It drills like it never stopped — a few long shifts, one full hopper of ore, and a shutdown sequence it performs with what reads as relief. You bank the load and power it down properly, the way somebody should have, eight years ago.

choices.text: Check the habitation pod first

outcome.narrative: The pod tells a short story: half a meal, one boot, a departure faster than boots. And on the console, a note, handwritten: 'Gone to flag down the med-ship. Rig's yours if I'm not back. —K.' Eight years. You take nothing. The claim beacon transmits all the way out of sensor range.

choices.text: Check the logbook: it mentions this rig

outcome.narrative: The logbook has a page on this rig. Its author met the owner, K, eight years ago: tired, friendly, coughing, waiting on a med-ship that was late. K gave them the restart code 'in case'. It still works. The rig runs one last shift and you bank the ore. In the habitation pod, under a coffee ring, a note in K's hand says what the logbook says: gone to flag down the med-ship.

choices.text: Respect the claim and move on

outcome.narrative: Expired or not, it's somebody's rig. You log its position for the registry — 'equipment intact, claimant absent' — and leave it holding its bite of rock. The law had an opinion. The tape on the renewal notice had a better one.

science_link.text: The ship computer notes that mining rocks like these is a real proposal, with real math, and realer skepticism.
science_link.label: Asteroid mining, seriously proposed

title: The Singing Rock

ai_flavor.aria: One of the asteroids is HUMMING! ARIA has matched the pitch! They're in harmony now! This is the best field ever!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV identifies the hum as piezoelectric resonance from compressed quartz veins. He delivers this explanation to a crew that has clearly already decided it's magic. He logs 'magic (piezoelectric).'
ai_flavor.rex: REX confirmed the humming rock is not a beacon, a lure, or a mine. It is a rock, humming. He has filed it under 'no action required' with unusual reluctance.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that novelty audio recordings sell well at stations! The rock's performance is unlicensed! The rock cannot sign! CHIP sees an opportunity in that!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has recorded forty minutes of the hum. Played at half speed, she notes, it resolves into something very like a chord progression. You'd know that if you'd listened to the copy she sent you.

body:
One of the asteroids is humming.

A low, steady tone, right at the edge of the sensors' hearing — solar heat working a quartz vein, physics doing an impression of a voice. The tone rises a little as the rock turns its face to the star, and falls as it turns away. Sunrise and sunset, rendered as a note.

The crew has been listening on the open channel for twenty minutes. Nobody has suggested moving on. You are, technically, behind schedule. The rock is, technically, singing.

choices.text: Drift alongside and listen a while

outcome.narrative: You match the rock's slow tumble and let it sing to the hull for an hour. No analysis, no sampling, no yield. Days later, crew members are still humming the note while they work — the field's one song, carried on in imperfect covers.

choices.text: Core a sample of the quartz

outcome.narrative: The drill takes a clean core of the singing vein. The tone drops a quarter-step and does not recover. The sample is scientifically excellent and worth real money, and the away team returns quieter than they left. Fair trade is a matter of ongoing internal debate.

choices.text: Record it for the ship's library

outcome.narrative: Forty minutes of asteroid, recorded clean, filed in the ship's library between the emergency drills and someone's audiobooks. It becomes the unofficial soundtrack of third watch. The rock, uncredited, achieves the widest audience of its four-billion-year career.

science_link.text: The ship computer files the explanation for the singing: compressed quartz making electricity. The effect is real, and it is called piezoelectricity.
science_link.label: Piezoelectricity: rocks that sing

title: The Shoal

ai_flavor.aria: Look at them all moving together! It's like a school of fish! Fish are friendly! These are rocks, but in spirit!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has modelled the shoal. Three thousand bodies, most of them small, all of them turning. He has found a line through. He notes the line is narrowing at a rate he would describe, if pressed, as brisk.
ai_flavor.rex: REX counts three thousand inbound contacts and zero hostiles. He finds the zero unconvincing. Point defense is warm. Point defense will not help.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's Collision Waiver covers impacts with up to one (1) object per voyage! You are about to exceed it! CHIP has pre-filed the paperwork!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY would go around. It costs fuel and days and nobody gets a story out of it. She suspects that's the part you object to.

body:
A shoal of rocks has drifted across your heading: a few thousand of them, none bigger than a house, all of them turning. They move together, the way fish do, for reasons that are entirely gravitational and look entirely deliberate.

There is a gap through the middle. It is closing. Most of the rocks are small. Small, at these speeds, is a relative term.

choices.text: Thread the gap at speed

outcome.narrative: You aim at the gap and go. The gap is narrower at the far end than it looked from the near one, which is how gaps work. Twelve points of hull, and one rock the size of a fist straight through the water tank, in a bang that everyone aboard will describe differently for the rest of their lives. {cost.water} points of water leave by the new hole before it is plugged.

choices.text: {crew.pilot} picks a line through

outcome.narrative: The pilot slows to a crawl and takes the shoal rock by rock, matching the tumble, never quite touching. Two days. Six points of fuel. One gentle scrape, which the pilot apologises to the ship for, out loud.

choices.text: Back out and go around

outcome.narrative: You turn and fly the long way round the shoal, which is very long, because the shoal is very wide. Four days, ten points of fuel and {cost.food} of food. Not one rock touches the ship. Dinner is smaller every night and nobody has anything to say about it, which was the point.

choices.text: Shields up and ride it out

outcome.narrative: You take the shield console and point the ship at the gap.

briefing.aria: Three thousand little rocks, all swimming our way! Raise the shields for every hit and they'll just bounce off!
briefing.marv: Three thousand bodies and one narrowing gap. The shields will take the impacts, provided they are up when each one arrives.
briefing.rex: Three thousand inbound contacts. Point defense is useless here. Shields are the only cover. Hold them on every flash.
briefing.chip: Your Collision Waiver covers one (1) rock! The shields cover the other two thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine!
briefing.ajoy: We're riding a shoal on shields, since going around was too dull. Keep them up when the rocks hit, ideally.

perfect.aria: Not one dent! Okay, a few scuffs! Scuffs are just the ship's way of saying it had fun!
perfect.marv: Three points of hull, all of it cosmetic, through a shoal of three thousand. I had not budgeted for this.
perfect.rex: Shoal crossed. Hull damage cosmetic. Shield discipline held under sustained fire.
perfect.chip: Barely a scuff! Your Collision Waiver stays unclaimed and fully renewable! Congratulations on not claiming!
perfect.ajoy: Scuffs only. Fine work, honestly. Going around would have saved the paint, but sure.

good.aria: The shields caught nearly everything! One rock got thirsty and visited the water tank, but we're through!
good.marv: Most impacts deflected. The ones that were not found the hull and the water tank, which is a talent of sorts.
good.rex: Through. Hull took hits in the gaps between shield cycles. One round in the water tank. Acceptable losses.
good.chip: Mostly deflected! The water tank counts as your one (1) covered collision! The hull dents are on you!
good.ajoy: Mostly held. You caught your breath right when the rocks didn't. The water tank noticed. Still, we're through.

poor.aria: The shields took a little nap halfway! The hull did all the work after that! What a brave hull!
poor.marv: The shields dropped mid-shoal and the hull handled the rest personally. So did the water tank, less successfully.
poor.rex: Shields down mid-crossing. Hull took direct fire the rest of the way. Water tank seam split. Long damage report.
poor.chip: Shield lapse mid-shoal! This exceeds your Collision Waiver by roughly everything! CHIP has pre-filed!
poor.ajoy: The shields dropped halfway and stayed down. I did suggest going around. I'll stop suggesting now. Probably.

perfect.narrative: You hold the shields through the thick of it, easing off between impacts and slamming them up on every flash. Three points of hull, all of it scuffs. The shoal closes behind you like a door.

good.narrative: The shields take most of it. Most is not all: seven points of hull got through in the seconds you were catching your breath, and one of them found the water tank, which lost {cost.water} more. The shoal closes behind you, unbothered.

poor.narrative: The shields drop mid-shoal. The rest of the crossing happens to the hull directly, at length: sixteen points of hull, and a split seam in the water tank that weeps {cost.water} more before anyone finds it. The crew spends the evening listening to the ship tick as it cools, counting.

title: The Rock Exhales

ai_flavor.aria: The asteroid is breathing! ARIA always knew rocks had feelings! It is a very big breath! She is sure it will finish soon!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV estimates the pocket held four billion years of frozen gas. He estimates it will finish venting at about the moment the spin becomes a problem. He has started a clock. He did not want to.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has identified the asteroid as the aggressor. It fired first. It is still firing. He recommends disengaging from the asteroid, a sentence he never expected to say.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes the anchor cable is rental equipment! Cutting it incurs a Non-Return Fee! CHIP will add it to the invoice! The invoice is getting long!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has her hand on the cable release. She isn't pulling it. She's just making it very clear that it's there.

body:
The anchor bit into the asteroid at 0400. At 0412 the asteroid exhaled.

Under the anchor point there was a pocket of frozen gas that had waited four billion years for someone to put a hole in it, and it has opinions. A white plume is venting past the hull, and the ship, still tethered, is beginning to turn with the rock. Slowly. Then less slowly.

choices.text: Cut the cable and burn clear

outcome.narrative: The cable goes with a twang you feel in your teeth, and you burn clear before the spin takes hold. Twelve points of fuel. The anchor stays in the rock, which now has a small monument to you sticking out of it. Nobody suggests going back for it.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} vents it down the drill shaft

outcome.narrative: The engineer feeds the plume back down the drill shaft and throttles it with a valve that was not designed for this and does it anyway. The spin stops. The shaft coughs up a load of loose ore on its way. The airlock cycled four times getting them in and out, and holding the ship steady while they worked burned a little fuel.

choices.text: Ride the spin until it runs out

outcome.narrative: You hold on. Everyone holds on. The spin climbs for an hour and then, as the pocket empties, winds down for another two, the tether groaning the whole time. Somebody lost their grip in the second hour and met a bulkhead. The galley lockers lost theirs in the first, and a week of stores went round the walls along with everyone's lunch.

choices.text: Cap the vent with a hull patch

outcome.narrative: You slap the patch over the vent, sticky side down, instructions side up. It holds. The rock goes quiet and stays quiet, wearing a small square of the ship's stores that will outlast everyone aboard. A little air got out while you worked.

title: Collision Cascade

ai_flavor.aria: Two asteroids met! And now there are thousands of little asteroids! That's how families work! ARIA is so happy for them!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV watched the collision. He has modelled the debris front. It expands at a rate he has written down and underlined twice. He notes that a cascade does not end. It only thins.
ai_flavor.rex: REX reports the largest coordinated inbound assault of his career. Thousands of projectiles. No command structure. No demands. He respects it. He would like to leave.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's Impact Protection™ is priced per impact! CHIP has done the arithmetic! CHIP recommends declaring bankruptcy now, while it's affordable!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has the scanner on wide sweep. There will be holes in that cloud and somebody has to find them fast. She'd rather not leave it to luck, which seems to be the plan so far.

body:
Two rocks the size of cities have met, a few thousand kilometers ahead, at a speed neither of them had planned for. There was no sound. There will be no sound. There is, instead, a cloud: a sphere of everything they were, expanding at several kilometers a second, and the ship is inside the radius it will reach in about twenty minutes.

The cloud is mostly gaps. The gaps are moving too.

choices.text: Scan for the gaps and fly them

outcome.narrative: You take the scanner and look for holes.

briefing.aria: The cloud is mostly gaps! We just have to find them and zoom through! I believe in us and in the gaps!
briefing.marv: The debris front expands at several kilometres a second and the gaps move with it. Lose one and the next is harder to find.
briefing.rex: Debris front inbound. Thousands of projectiles. Find the holes, call the turns. There is no second pass.
briefing.chip: Every gap you find is an impact you don't pay for! Impact Protection™ is priced per hit, so find lots!
briefing.ajoy: There are holes in that cloud. Somebody has to stay on them, since luck seems to be the backup plan.

perfect.aria: Swerve, swerve, swerve, through! My tummy is upside down but we're out! The gaps loved us!
perfect.marv: Every gap found. Three points of hull. The cascade carries on behind us, more or less forever. We do not.
perfect.rex: Front penetrated through the gaps. Minimal damage. That was precision work under fire.
perfect.chip: Barely a scratch! At per-impact pricing, that's practically a rebate! Impact Protection™ salutes you!
perfect.ajoy: Every gap, in order. I'll admit it. The swerving could have been gentler, but I'll admit it.

good.aria: We found almost all the gaps! The ones we missed gave the hull a big loud hug, but we're through!
good.marv: Most gaps found. The misses were concentrated in one loud second near the end. Statistics are like that.
good.rex: Through the front. Missed gaps cost hull, most of it in one long hit near the exit.
good.chip: Through the front! Each missed gap is billed separately under Impact Protection™! Itemised invoice to follow!
good.ajoy: Most of the gaps. Near the end you stopped finding them, and the hull noticed. Still, we're out.

poor.aria: We lost the gaps and went through anyway! The hull took a real beating, but we're out the other side!
poor.marv: The scanner lost the gaps halfway. We crossed the rest blind. The hull kept count so we would not have to.
poor.rex: Lost the gaps. Went through blind. Heavy hull damage, crew shaken. Not a repeatable tactic.
poor.chip: Went through blind! At per-impact pricing, that was the most expensive twenty minutes in company history!
poor.ajoy: Lost the gaps halfway and flew the rest blind. I'd have stayed on them. Ask the hull how that went.

perfect.narrative: You lock onto the gaps one after another and call the turns, and the ship slips through the front in a run of hard, sickening swerves. Three points of hull, four of fuel. Behind you the cloud keeps going, and will for a long time.

good.narrative: You find most of the gaps. The ones you miss find the ship instead: ten points of hull, most of it in one long, loud second near the end.

poor.narrative: The scanner loses the gaps halfway through and the ship goes through the front blind. Twenty-two points of hull. Everyone aboard can now say, accurately, that they were caught in an asteroid collision. Nobody wants to.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} turns the cargo doors into a shield

outcome.narrative: The engineer unbolts the cargo doors, swings them out on the crane arms and angles them into the front like two very expensive umbrellas. The debris hits the doors, which is the idea. Eight points of hull get round the edges. With enough hands the doors go back on quickly; without them, it is days of hammering.

choices.text: Hide behind the biggest fragment

outcome.narrative: You tuck in behind the largest piece of what used to be a city-sized rock and let it take the front. It takes the front. It also spins, which nobody had fully thought about, and the ship spends four days dodging its own shelter. Eight points of fuel, ten of hull.

choices.text: Turn back the way you came

outcome.narrative: You turn round and burn hard back down your own track, then round the edge of the front the very long way. Four days. The cloud never catches you. The fuel gauge does: a third of the tank, gone into running away.

choices.text: Punch straight through the front

outcome.narrative: You aim for the middle and go through at full speed, on the theory that less time inside is less time being hit. The theory is half right. Twenty-eight points of hull, and one fragment that came through the plating into a cabin that was occupied.

science_link.text: The ship computer files a reference: collisions that make debris that makes more collisions have a name, and the people who keep satellites flying around Earth worry about it a great deal.
science_link.label: Collision cascades

title: Loose Gravel

ai_flavor.aria: The poor little probe! It's stuck in a ball pit! ARIA wants to rescue it! ARIA also wants to try the ball pit!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV reads the rock as a rubble pile, loose debris holding together under its own very weak gravity. It is less a rock than a suggestion of one. He advises anchoring to something else.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has checked the probe for a beacon, a charge or a trap. It is a probe. It is stuck. He is almost disappointed.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can see the probe's maker's logo! The company still exists! It will want its probe back! CHIP will be happy to negotiate a finder's fee! For the probe! In its own logo!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes that the probe has been blinking that light for years. Someone built it to call for help, and then landed it on gravel. She'd have checked the surface first. Just noting.

body:
There is a mining probe half-buried in one of the rocks.

It did not crash. It landed, very gently, and then kept going: down into the asteroid as if into a ball pit, until only its antenna and one slightly embarrassed status light were left above the surface.

The rock is not really a rock. It is a pile of gravel and boulders held together by little more than the good manners of its own gravity, and the probe found this out the hard way.

choices.text: Send a tethered team down for the probe

briefing.aria: The team's on tethers and the gravel is flying! Catch every bit of probe they dig loose before it floats off!
briefing.marv: A rubble pile. Every scoop lifts gravel and probe together, then slides back. How much probe comes up is what we catch.
briefing.rex: Team's tethered and digging. Surface is unstable. Recover the probe in pieces before the pile slides back.
briefing.chip: Every piece of that probe is salvage! Its maker's logo is still on it, which I consider a selling point!
briefing.ajoy: They're digging in gravel that slides back. Pull up what they free, quickly. I'd have checked the surface first, but sure.

perfect.aria: The whole probe came up! And the little light finally got to rest! Everybody did amazing!
perfect.marv: Probe recovered whole: plating, drill head, wiring. The status light has stopped blinking. It seemed relieved.
perfect.rex: Probe recovered intact. No beacon, no charge, no trap. Stripped for parts. Clean op.
perfect.chip: The whole probe, logo and all! Plating, drill head and wiring, ready to strip! Finders Keepers®!
perfect.ajoy: All of it, in one piece. Even I can't fault that. The light finally went off, which I think we all needed.

good.aria: We got most of the probe! The gravel kept a little bit as a souvenir! And someone kept the light!
good.marv: Most of the probe recovered, which is enough to strip for metal. The gravel kept the remainder, as gravel does.
good.rex: Partial recovery. Most of the hardware up before the pile slid back. Usable metal. Good enough.
good.chip: Most of a probe! That's still mostly salvage! The blinking light ships as a free collectible!
good.ajoy: Most of it. The gravel took the rest back while you were deciding. Still, it's metal.

poor.aria: We got the antenna and some wire! And a lot of grit! Grit is just tiny rocks being friendly!
poor.marv: Recovered: one antenna, some wire, considerable grit. The rubble pile kept the rest, as rubble piles do.
poor.rex: Pile kept collapsing. Recovered antenna and wire only. Team's back up, gritty. No casualties.
poor.chip: An antenna and a handful of wire! Grit removal is not covered! I can recommend a laundry service!
poor.ajoy: An antenna and some wire. I'd have checked the surface first. The grit is in everything now, just noting.

perfect.narrative: The team goes down on tethers and digs the probe out like a dog digging out a ball, gravel floating up around them in slow clouds. It comes up whole. The hull plating, the drill head and its little wiring loom are all worth stripping, and the status light, unplugged at last, goes out with what everyone agrees was relief.

good.narrative: The team frees most of the probe before the gravel slides back over the rest. What comes up is enough to strip for metal. The status light comes up too, still blinking. Someone keeps it.

poor.narrative: Every scoop brings down more gravel than it lifts. The team comes back up two days later with the probe's antenna, a handful of wire and a great deal of grit in places grit should not be.

outcome.narrative: A tethered team goes down after the probe.

choices.text: Snag the antenna with the grapple

outcome.narrative: Three passes with the grapple and it catches. The antenna comes away clean; the probe stays down. You get a length of good metal for the fuel it took to hold position. The status light, now attached to nothing, keeps blinking all the way to the cargo bay.

choices.text: Leave it; nothing about that rock looks solid

outcome.narrative: Nothing about the rock looks safe to stand on, and nothing about the probe looks worth sinking for. You log its position for the maker and move on. The status light blinks after you, patiently, the way it has for years.

science_link.text: Many small asteroids are rubble piles: loose gravel held together by gravity. When NASA's OSIRIS-REx touched the asteroid Bennu in 2020, its sampling arm sank in as if into a ball pit.
science_link.label: Rubble-pile asteroids

title: Prime Orbital Real Estate

ai_flavor.aria: A HOUSE! In SPACE! With a VIEW! ARIA has always wanted a house! ARIA understands she lives in the ship! It's not the same!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has reviewed the sales pitch. The 'stunning views' are of other rocks. The 'easy commute' is to nowhere. The 'low fees' are, technically, accurate, because the company is gone and nobody is collecting them.
ai_flavor.rex: REX reports the sign is drawing more power than the beacon. Someone wired it to last. They did a good job. On the wrong thing.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP LOVES this sign! CHIP has never felt so understood! CHIP would like a moment!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY points out that the sign is made of good metal and nobody is going to buy this rock. She leaves the conclusion to you.

body:
A large rock in the field is wearing a sign.

It is lit. It is enormous. It says LUXURY ESTATE · STUNNING VIEWS · AVAILABLE NOW, above a contact code for a company that went bankrupt before your grandparents were born. A beacon under the sign plays a sales pitch on a loop, in a voice that is still very excited about the 'quiet neighbourhood'.

There are no neighbours. That was the whole selling point.

choices.text: Strip the sign for parts

outcome.narrative: It takes two days to take the sign down, letter by letter. The frame is good metal, the lettering is good scrap, and the beacon makes its pitch right up until the moment you cut its power, mid-sentence, on the word 'opportunity'. The ship computer observes a moment of silence. Nobody else does.

choices.text: Answer the sales pitch

outcome.narrative: You open a channel and ask about the rock. The recorded salesman, who has waited three generations for this, is thrilled. He walks you through the rock's features (rock), its amenities (also rock) and the financing (rock-based). The crew asks follow-up questions for an hour. It's the most fun anyone has had in weeks.

choices.text: Leave the sign lit

outcome.narrative: You leave it lit. It isn't hurting anyone, and out here a light is a light. As the field falls behind, the sign is the last thing on the scope: AVAILABLE NOW, for whoever comes next. Someone salutes it. It isn't clear whether they're joking.

title: Tail Lights

ai_flavor.aria: A COMET! With a TAIL! ARIA has wanted to see one since before ARIA was installed! ARIA was installed eleven months ago! It still counts!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes the tail points away from the star, not behind the comet's path. The star's wind pushes it. The comet is, strictly, being blown about. He finds this relatable.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has plotted the dust density in the tail. Fine particles. The hull will be polished, not punctured. He is permitting it.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP would like to offer comet-tail ice as a luxury product! Four billion years old! Never been opened! Slightly dirty!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the ice is mostly water. Also some of the oldest material in the system. She'd take a little of both. Not that it's her call.

body:
A comet is passing through the field.

It is small, as comets go: a dirty snowball a few kilometres across, falling in toward a star it will not reach for years. But it has started to wake up. Gas and dust are boiling off its sunward face, and its tail streams out behind it for a hundred thousand kilometres, glowing, pointing straight away from the light like a weathervane in a solar wind.

The ship is close enough to fly through the edge of it.

choices.text: Skim ice from the tail

outcome.narrative: Two days running alongside the comet with the collector scoops open. The ice comes in grey and gritty and melts down to water as clean as any you have had. The filter keeps a small jar of the grit. Somebody labels it 'older than everything'.

choices.text: Fly the ship through the tail

outcome.narrative: You fly straight through the edge of the tail. For twenty minutes the viewports glitter, every window full of tiny lights blowing past the wrong way, and the hull hisses softly under it like rain on a tent. The crew watches the whole way through without anyone saying a word.

choices.text: Xenobiologist bags the dust

outcome.narrative: {crew.xenobiologist} spends two days in a suit at the cargo airlock catching dust on sticky plates, and comes back in with three plates of grime and a grin. Comet dust carries organic molecules, the building blocks of the chemistry of life, delivered by snowball. One sample is worth something to any lab. The grin is not for sale.

science_link.text: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun, pushed by sunlight and the solar wind, so a comet heading outward travels tail-first.
science_link.label: Comet tails
